cards.explanation: The answer is that the idols of Egypt will tremble before Him. The verse says, “The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him…” Think about that for a second. Idols, and they're the ones shaking. The LORD shows up on a swift cloud and the idols tremble before Him.
The word is melt, friends. The verse says the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. That's fear. I'd rather be a chocolate chip in a warm oven than a heart doing that.

The answer is idols and spirits of the dead. The LORD says they will “…resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists.” (Isaiah 19:3) Their plans are frustrated, so that's where they turn. The verse lists it out: idols, spirits of the dead, mediums and spiritists.

The word is harsh, friends. The Lord GOD of Hosts says He will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of a harsh master, and a fierce king will rule over them. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage. It's plain words about a hard time coming.

The answer is that the waters of the Nile will dry up. The verse says, “The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty.” Those are plain words for a river that has lost its water. The next verses go on to say the canals will stink and the reeds and rushes will wither.

The answer is False. Verse 8 says the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. Mourning, lamenting and pining away are the opposite of celebrating. Sad folks, not party folks.

The answer is that the message dares them to reveal what the LORD has planned. It says, “Let them tell you and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt.” So the counselors claim wisdom, and the message asks them to show it. It's like someone who says they know the recipe, so I say: bake the thing. The question stays hanging in the air.

The answer is that the LORD poured it into her. The text says, “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion.” It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly. The confusion in Egypt's leaders doesn't come from anywhere else in this verse.

The answer is True, friends. The verse says, “There is nothing Egypt can do…” and then adds head or tail, palm or reed. That covers everybody, from the top to the bottom. It's a closed door on every side. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, so let's let it sit a moment.

The answer is Judah, friends. The verse says the land of Judah will bring terror to Egypt. Whenever Judah is mentioned, Egypt will tremble over what the LORD of Hosts has planned against it. Imagine hearing one name and your knees start knocking.
The answer is the LORD of Hosts. Verse 18 says five cities in Egypt will “…swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts.” Whole cities are pledging themselves to Him. What a turn.

The answer is True, friends. Verse 20 says, “When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them.” Egyptians cry out, and the LORD sends a rescuer. That's the whole exchange, right there in the text.

The answer is False. The verse says the LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD. They worship with sacrifices and offerings. After all that trembling, this is quite a change.

The answer is that He will heal them. The verse says, “He will strike them but heal them.” Then it adds that they will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them. The strike isn't the last word in this verse. The healing is.

The word is worship, friends. The verse says, “The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together.” Just before that, the text says there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, with the Assyrians going to Egypt and the Egyptians to Assyria. Two groups worshiping side by side is a picture worth looking at twice.

The answer is that He speaks of them as His own. The LORD says, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Egypt is called His people, and Assyria is called His handiwork. That's a whole lot of belonging in one sentence.
